newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army problems pile up, minister goes east.
newsitem.headline: Russian army problems pile up, minister goes east.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov faced a threat of new protests by civilians employed by the army on Wednesday as he began a tour of under-funded forces in Russia's far east.
Rodionov flew to the Kamchatka peninsula and was due on Thursday to visit Vladivostok, home of Russia's Pacific Fleet and heart of a region which is particularly badly hit by financial problems.

On a day of bad news for Rodionov, the Defence Ministry daily Krasnaya Zvezvda said an unusually low number of new recruits was expected under the autumn call-up and another newspaper reported an increase in crime in the military.
In another blow, civilian workers employed by the armed forces threatened a day of protests on October 31 to urge the government to pay off months of unpaid wages.

"The trades unions of construction workers in the armed forces and workers with the Navy are organising protests on October 31 to last one hour to 24 hours," said Spartak Arzhavkin, head of the civilian workers' trade union.
He told Interfax news agency that the government owed his union members more than 5.5 trillion roubles ($1 billion) in unpaid wages.

Vladivostok was one of the main cities hit by similar protests a month ago. Civilian employees of the Pacific Fleet staged a one-day protest and workers who supply the navy blocked the main entrance to the Fleet's headquarters.
Rodionov's trip gives him a chance to check the combat readiness of his forces in a distant region and get a first-hand look at the problems they are facing.
Russian troops complain they are underfed, poorly clothed and face delays in getting paid.

Army spending has dropped drastically since the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991 and many troops are demoralised by the poor showing against rebel guerrillas in breakaway Chechnya. Security chief Alexander Lebed fears troops could mutiny soon.
Other military chiefs dismiss the threat of a mutiny, and there are signs that hard lobbying by Lebed and Rodionov is starting to bear fruit.

President Boris Yeltsin has made army reforms a priority and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin proposed a new tax on Tuesday to help the army. He has also promised to revise planned spending on the army under the draft 1997 budget.

But most of the news continues to be bleak. Krasnaya Zvezda said 215,000 youngsters were being called up this autumn for national service but that the figure represented only 13.3 percent of men of call-up age.

This compared with 21 percent last spring and an average of 50 to 85 percent in France, Spain and Turkey, it said, and attributed the fall largely to new exemptions for students. The extent of draft-dodging, notoriously high, was not clear.
The Defence Ministry declined comment on the report.

The pro-Yeltsin newspaper Rossiiskiye Vesti said the number of criminal cases opened against military personnel had risen to 672 in the first six months of this year -- 39 more than in the first half of 1995.

"Such crimes are being committed not only by ordinary soldiers or sergeants, but by warrant officers, and other officers including senior ones," deputy chief military prosecutor Stanislav Gaveto told the newspaper.
Weapon-stealing from the army had doubled, the paper said.
An annual report on the world's military by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), released on Wednesday, promised more trouble ahead for Russia.
"The decline in capability in all departments of the Russian armed forces seems set to continue," the IISS report said.
